title: The old strings return
hook: musicians are reviving the rebab, saranda and taus for kirtan

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gurmukhi, and your line was the word online. Did you look up one ang? Today the newest tool steps back, and some of the oldest come forward. Day one thousand forty.

A wooden case clicks open on a classroom floor. Inside is an instrument shaped a little like a lute, with a skin-covered belly and a short neck. A teacher lifts it out the way you'd lift a sleeping baby, tunes it slowly, and plucks one string. The note is low and dry, and it hangs in the air a long time. A row of students with harmoniums on their laps goes quiet. Some of them have never heard one played in person. This sound, Sikh tradition says, was there at the very start of kirtan. Today, the old strings return.
screen: `A WOODEN CASE CLICKS OPEN.` → `ONE LOW, DRY NOTE.` → `THERE AT THE START.`

segments.voice: First, the rabab. Sikh tradition remembers Bhai Mardana, Guru Nanak's companion on his long journeys, playing the rabab while the Guru sang. Guru Nanak's hymns were first heard, tradition says, over strings like these. Second, the other strings. Tradition links the saranda, a bowed instrument, to Guru Arjan, and the taus, a bowed instrument carved in the shape of a peacock, to Guru Hargobind. Each carries a Guru's name in the tradition's memory. Third, the quiet and the return. Over time, the harmonium, a later arrival, became the familiar sound of kirtan in gurdwaras. It's easy to carry and easy to learn, and it carries hymns beautifully. But the old strings grew rare. Now musicians and teachers are bringing them back: building rababs and tauses again, teaching the raags the hymns are set in, and playing kirtan the older way. Some sangats welcome it. Some love the harmonium they grew up with. Both are kirtan. Fourth, the root. In Raag Asa, at Ang 350, Guru Nanak names the instrument underneath every instrument: let understanding be your instrument, and love your drum. Then bliss comes, and the mind is always eager. A string can be revived. A raag can be relearned. But what makes it kirtan is the listening heart behind it. That's today's line: old strings return. Not to replace anything. To remind everyone where the song began.
screen: `BHAI MARDANA'S RABAB.` · `SARANDA AND TAUS.` · `THE HARMONIUM, AND THE REVIVAL.` · `UNDERSTANDING THE INSTRUMENT, LOVE THE DRUM.` · then, large: `OLD STRINGS RETURN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of listening. If you can, play a recording of kirtan on a string instrument, softly. If not, just listen to the room: the hum of a fridge, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Sit, and don't name the sounds. Let them arrive and fade, the way a plucked string fades. Breathe in as a sound begins. Breathe out as it ends. Notice the space between notes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Rabab. The stringed instrument tradition links to Bhai Mardana, now revived along with the saranda and the taus, so kirtan can be heard the older way. Today's word.
Your line: old strings return. Today, listen to one piece of music played on a string instrument, all the way through, without doing anything else. Day one thousand forty.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, kirtan is usually sung with harmonium and tabla. Some Sikh musicians and teachers now also teach and perform kirtan on string instruments such as the rabab, saranda, taus and dilruba, in the raags the hymns are set in.

notes: Ang 350 ('vaaja mat pakhaavaj bhaao, hoe anand sadaa man chaao') is paraphrased; please confirm the Ang and the wording.
The links of the saranda to Guru Arjan and the taus to Guru Hargobind are given as tradition; please confirm these attributions as commonly taught in Gurmat Sangeet.
'The harmonium, a later arrival' gives no date on purpose; please confirm the framing is fair and doesn't diminish harmonium kirtan.
howItsDone says kirtan in gurdwaras is usually sung with harmonium and tabla; confirm.
Hook describes the rabab as lute-like with a skin-covered belly; confirm the description.

Editor pass: the Ang 350 paraphrase now renders vaaja as instrument, not music, and names the Ang in the teach; the garbled screen head (UNDERSTANDING YOUR MUSIC) fixed to match; the hook no longer tells the listener what they expect.

Audit pass: 'the hymns we've been reading on screens were first heard over strings like these' overstated (most of the Granth's hymns are by later Gurus and bhagats); now limited to Guru Nanak's hymns. 'A voice from the Gurus' own houses' replaced with a plainer tradition line.
